sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>jacobian positions</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">J11   J12</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">J21   J22</text></svg>
sections.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 array labeled as a Jacobian.
sections.body_md:
A vector-valued map has one scalar output per row. The Jacobian is the matrix whose \(i\)-th row is the gradient of the \(i\)-th output, written as a row. If there are \(m\) outputs and \(n\) inputs, the matrix is \(m \times n\). For a single output the Jacobian is the gradient transposed into a row.

The chain rule multiplies these matrices. For a composition, evaluate the outer Jacobian at the image of the inner map, evaluate the inner Jacobian at the original input, and multiply with the outer factor on the left. The image point matters: the outer derivative has no reason to be evaluated at the original input.

When the outer function is scalar, the same multiplication writes the gradient of the composition as the transpose of the inner Jacobian times the outer gradient at the image. The transpose appears because this page keeps gradients as columns and Jacobians with outputs as rows.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The entry and the two chain-rule forms are
\[
(J_F)_{ij} = \frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x_j}, \qquad J_{F \circ G}(x) = J_F(G(x))\, J_G(x),
\]
\[
\nabla (f \circ g)(x) = J_g(x)^{T}\, \nabla f(g(x)).
\]
The first product is \(m \times n\) when \(F\) has \(m\) outputs and \(G\) has \(n\) inputs. The transpose keeps the scalar chain rule the same shape as a column gradient.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(F(x, y) = (x + y,\ 6x)\) and let the inner map send \(t\) to \((6 + t,\ -2 + t)\). At \(t = 0\) the image is the inner point (6, -2), and the inner velocity is \((1, 1)\). The Jacobian of \(F\) is constant,
\[
J_F = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 6 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The product with the velocity is \((2, 6)\). The first output along the path is \((6 + t) + (-2 + t) = 4 + 2t\), whose derivative is 2, matching the first entry. The second output is \(6(6 + t)\), whose derivative is 6, matching the second entry. The outer Jacobian did not need a special point because it is constant, but the chain rule still evaluates it at the image.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Rows and columns are part of the definition. Transposing by habit changes the shape. The outer Jacobian is evaluated at the image, not at the input. Matrix multiplication is not entrywise multiplication, and composition does not add Jacobians; addition is the rule for a sum of maps. For a scalar outer function, dropping the transpose on the inner Jacobian disagrees with the column convention as soon as the dimensions differ.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Gradients of \(x^{T} A x\) and of a squared residual are chain-rule calculations with these shapes. A computational graph applies the same product one elementary step at a time. Newton's method for a nonlinear system solves the linear model \(F(x) + J_F(x)(z - x) = 0\), which is this Jacobian used as the derivative of a map.
